headings.title: Operating Room Environment and Zoning
headings.content:
The operating room suite operates under a strict zoning system designed to control microbial contamination and protect vulnerable surgical patients from healthcare-associated infections. Facility design typically divides the department into three distinct zones based on cleanliness requirements and attire mandates.

- **Restricted Zone**: Includes the actual operating rooms and sterile core areas where sterile supplies are stored. Personnel must wear complete surgical attire, including scrub suits, caps that fully cover head hair, and surgical masks that cover both nose and mouth.
- **Semi-Restricted Zone**: Comprises peripheral corridors, instrument processing areas, and recovery spaces. Scrub attire and hair covers are mandatory here, but masks are generally optional unless sterile items are actively exposed.
- **Unrestricted Zone**: Serves as the entrance and transition point for patients, staff, and administrative visitors. Street clothes are permitted in this zone, separated from clinical areas by physical barriers or adhesive tacky mats.

headings.title: Aseptic Technique and Sterile Field Maintenance
headings.content:
Aseptic technique forms the bedrock of surgical nursing, encompassing every practice that maintains items and areas free from pathogenic microorganisms. Once sterile drapes are placed around the surgical site, they establish a boundary known as the sterile field. Only sterilized items, equipment, and personnel who have completed a surgical scrub may cross this boundary.

Maintaining this environment requires constant vigilance regarding proximity and movement. Scrubbed personnel must pass each other face-to-face or back-to-back to avoid accidental contact between unsterile and sterile garment areas. Gowns are considered sterile only from the chest to the level of the sterile field, and sleeves from two inches above the elbow to the cuffs. Unscrubbed team members must always face the sterile field when passing it and maintain a distance of at least one foot to prevent accidental contamination. Any sterile package dropped below waist level or suspected of being compromised is immediately discarded.

headings.title: Surgical Scrubbing, Gowning, and Gloving
headings.content:
Before touching sterile items, surgical team members must remove transient microorganisms and significantly reduce resident flora through a rigorous surgical hand scrub. Unlike standard handwashing, the surgical scrub extends from the fingertips up to two inches above the elbows using an antimicrobial agent, typically chlorhexidine gluconate or povidone-iodine, combined with mechanical friction.

Following the scrub, hands and arms are dried with a sterile towel using an aseptic technique where the towel touches only one arm before being discarded. The scrub nurse or surgeon then dons a sterile gown using the closed-glove technique, ensuring the hands never pass outside the gown's cuff edges during glove placement. Closed gloving minimizes skin exposure and remains the gold standard for reducing surgical site infections.

headings.title: Surgical Safety Checklists and Patient Verification
headings.content:
Surgical errors, including wrong-site or wrong-patient procedures, represent catastrophic yet entirely preventable events in clinical practice. The World Health Organization (WHO) Surgical Safety Checklist provides a standardized communication framework utilized globally and across Nigerian tertiary hospitals to safeguard patients through three distinct phases: Sign In, Time Out, and Sign Out.

- **Sign In**: Occurs before anesthesia induction with the nurse, anesthetist, and patient (if awake) verifying identity, surgical site, procedure, and consent.
- **Time Out**: Conducted immediately before skin incision. All operating room activity stops, and team members actively verify patient identity, exact surgical site, antibiotic prophylaxis timing, and essential imaging availability.
- **Sign Out**: Performed before the patient leaves the operating room, confirming final counts of instruments and sponges, specimen labeling, and recovery priorities.

headings.title: Intraoperative Positioning and Skin Preparation
headings.content:
Proper patient positioning safeguards physiological function and prevents nerve damage or pressure injuries during prolonged anesthesia. Common positions include supine, lithotomy, prone, and lateral decubitus, each carrying specific physiological challenges. For instance, the lithotomy position requires careful, synchronized lowering of both legs to prevent sudden hemodynamic drops and lumbar strain, while pressure points must be padded with gel or foam to avoid peripheral nerve palsies such as ulnar or peroneal nerve injury.

Following positioning, skin preparation aims to reduce the microbial count on the patient's skin rapidly. The scrub nurse or circulator applies antiseptic agents, such as chlorhexidine gluconate in alcohol or povidone-iodine, starting at the planned incision site and working outward in concentric circles toward the periphery. Once contaminated areas like the umbilicus or groin are reached, sponges are discarded to prevent tracking bacteria back into the clean incision zone.

headings.title: Instrument, Sponge, and Needle Accountability
headings.content:
Retained surgical items represent a severe medical error and a preventable cause of postoperative morbidity. Preventing this requires rigorous, structured counting protocols performed collaboratively by the scrub nurse and the circulating nurse. Counts are conducted audibly and visibly at specific intervals: at baseline before surgery begins, when closure of a cavity or deep layer starts, when subcutaneous closure begins, and finally during skin closure.

All sponges, sharps (needles and blades), and miscellaneous instruments must be accounted for before the surgical team closes the wound. If any count discrepancy occurs, the surgeon must immediately halt closure while the entire room is searched, including the sterile field, trash receptacles, and linen hampers. If necessary, portable intraoperative X-ray imaging is performed to rule out a retained item before the patient leaves the operating room.

headings.title: Infection Control and Hazard Management in the OR
headings.content:
The operating room environment presents unique occupational and patient safety hazards that require strict adherence to infection control policies. Sharps safety is paramount; surgical blades and needles should never be passed by hand directly. Instead, surgical teams utilize a designated neutral zone or 'no-hands zone' on a sterile basin where instruments are placed and retrieved to prevent sharps injuries and bloodborne pathogen transmission like HIV and Hepatitis B.

Environmental hygiene relies on standard precautions, proper biomedical waste segregation, and appropriate personal protective equipment. Waste segregation in Nigerian hospitals dictates that infectious materials, such as blood-soaked gauze, go into yellow bins, while sharps go into puncture-proof safety boxes. Following each procedure, housekeeping personnel perform terminal cleaning of horizontal surfaces, surgical lights, and anesthesia equipment to eliminate residual bioburden before the next case.
